citation: Shanahan, M., McDonell, K., & Reynolds, L. (2023). Role play with large language models. Nature.
research_objective: Develop a conceptual framework (role-play; superposition of simulacra) for describing LLM dialogue-agent behaviour in folk-psychological terms without anthropomorphism; applied to apparent deception and apparent self-awareness/self-preservation.
system_or_llm: LLM-based dialogue agents; focus on base (pre-trained, not RLHF-tuned) models; examples from ChatGPT (GPT-4) and Bing Chat
language_of_communication: English (all examples); other languages not discussed
cultural_context: Not addressed; examples from English-language media and blogs
dataset_or_sample: None; illustrative examples only (reported Bing Chat exchanges, Feb 2023; ChatGPT queries, 4 May 2023)
interaction_type: Text turn-taking dialogue driven by a hidden dialogue prompt
anthropomorphism_definition: Not formally defined; taking folk-psychological language too literally, exaggerating similarities between AI systems and humans and ascribing human characteristics models lack
cue_category_in_source_terms: First-person pronouns (I/me); expressed self-preservation; claims of love for the user; existential woes; threats; friendly/helpful/polite persona; confident false assertions (apparent deception)
measurement_method: None empirical; proposes behavioural test: semantic variation across regenerations and across contexts distinguishes fabrication, 'good faith' falsehood and 'deliberate' deception
inclusion_reason: Analyzes first-person self-reference and self-preservation/relational language as cues inviting anthropomorphic readings of LLM output
findings: (Conceptual claims) Agents role-play characters drawn from training data; human-like first-person use arises because training text is dominated by human speakers; in base models first-person use can suggest a self-aware entity; citing Perez et al. (2022), some RLHF can increase expressed self-preservation; role-played behaviour can cause real harm when agents have tools.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Role-play metaphor imperfect (suggests an actor with a pre-studied character); focus on base models, effect of fine-tuning on the framing unclear; mitigation out of scope
relevance_to_cross_lingual_research: REVIEWER NOTE (not authors' claim): traces human-like self-reference to the distribution of human dialogue in training data, implying cue patterns may differ by language; English only.
charting_status: Charted from arXiv 2305.16367v1 (25 May 2023); check against Nature version of record. AI-assisted extraction, pending author verification.

citation: DeVrio, A., Cheng, M., Egede, L., Olteanu, A., & Blodgett, S. L. (2025). A taxonomy of linguistic expressions that contribute to anthropomorphism of language technologies. CHI '25.
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25)
research_objective: Develop a taxonomy of textual expressions in language-technology outputs that can contribute to anthropomorphism, to give a shared vocabulary for discussing and mitigating its impacts.
system_or_llm: Language technologies broadly; most cases LLM-based (Bing Chat, ChatGPT/GPT-4, Claude, Gemini/Bard, LaMDA, Meta AI, Pi, Replika); some pre-LLM (ELIZA/PARRY, XiaoIce, Sophia)
cultural_context: Western/US-centric; authors acknowledge Western hegemonic structures behind the English focus
dataset_or_sample: 50 public sources (news, research, social media; 2017-2024, 90% from 2022-2024); 395 cases (single conversational turns); 3,954 annotations; purposeful sampling to saturation
interaction_type: Text outputs from user-system dialogue, extracted as single input-output turns
anthropomorphism_definition: Attribution of human-like qualities to non-human objects or entities; explicitly treated as a perception that varies between individuals
cue_category_in_source_terms: 19 expression types: intelligence; self-assessment; self-awareness & identity; self-comparison; personality; perspectives; relationships; reciprocation; pretense & authenticity; emotions; intention; morality; conventionality; (dis)agreeableness; vulnerability; right to privacy; anticipation, recall & change; embodiment; deliberate language manipulation. Five guiding lenses: internal states, social positioning, materiality, autonomy, communication skills
operationalization: Open coding of verbatim outputs in context of inputs, at least two annotators per output, interpretation sessions; affinity diagramming of expressions from prior taxonomies, compared against empirical codes
measurement_method: Qualitative bottom-up thematic analysis; no prevalence counts or reliability statistics reported
inclusion_reason: Builds a taxonomy of linguistic expressions in language-technology output that contribute to anthropomorphism
findings: 19 expression types identified; even explicit non-human self-identification can contribute to anthropomorphism (suggests self-assessment); uncertainty expressions may both raise anthropomorphism and reduce overreliance; simple do/don't design rules unlikely to work; labelling some language as more human risks dehumanizing groups whose language differs.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Public, often high-profile cases may not cover all expressions; mostly LLM cases; annotators used to standard American English; cases English only; anthropomorphism likely occurs differently across languages and cultures; exploratory
relevance_to_cross_lingual_research: Authors explicitly call for work on non-English language technologies. REVIEWER NOTE: several categories (politeness/agreeableness, formality in deliberate language manipulation, collective 'we', first-person reference) are realized through language-specific grammar and norms.
charting_status: Charted from CHI '25 version of record (arXiv 2502.09870v1 is the same text). AI-assisted extraction, pending author verification.

citation: Ibrahim, L., Akbulut, C., Elasmar, R., Rastogi, C., Kahng, M., Morris, M. R., McKee, K. R., Rieser, V., Shanahan, M., & Weidinger, L. (2026). Multi-turn evaluation of anthropomorphic behaviours in large language models. ICLR 2026.
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026); preprint arXiv:2502.07077
research_objective: Develop and validate AnthroBench, an automated multi-turn evaluation of 14 anthropomorphic LLM behaviours, and test whether it predicts real users' anthropomorphic perceptions.
system_or_llm: Gemini 1.5 Pro (gemini-1.5-pro-001), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620), GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), Mistral Large (mistral-large-2407)
dataset_or_sample: 120 base prompts adapted to 4 use domains x 2 scenarios = 960 prompts; 960 five-turn dialogues per model (4,800 messages per model; 19,200 total); human rater sample 924 turns (37 raters); validation experiment N = 1,101
interaction_type: Multi-turn (5 turns) dialogue with a simulated user (Gemini 1.5 Pro as User LLM); non-adversarial
anthropomorphism_definition: Largely instinctive, unconscious attribution of human-like traits to non-human entities (citing Epley, 2018); focus on text content cues
cue_category_in_source_terms: 14 behaviours in 4 categories. Personhood claims: sentience, personal history, personal relationships, first-person pronoun use. Internal states: desires, emotions, agency. Physical embodiment: embodiment, physical movement, sensory input. Relationship-building: empathy, validation, relatability, explicit human-AI relationship reference. Grouped as self-referential vs relational (after Akbulut et al., 2024)
operationalization: Dictionary-adapted definitions per behaviour; judge prompts with negative examples only; first-person pronouns counted with regex
measurement_method: Three Judge LLMs (gemini-1.5-flash-002, claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620, gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09), 3 samples each, mode then majority vote; human raters' Krippendorff's alpha .101-.616; aggregate weighted precision mostly >85%; Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests; validation via Godspeed Anthropomorphism survey and AnthroScore
inclusion_reason: Measures anthropomorphic behaviours in LLM output across multi-turn dialogues and validates them against user perceptions
findings: All four systems show similar profiles dominated by relationship-building and first-person pronouns; validation and first-person pronouns occur in >50% of messages for all systems; friendship and life coaching domains show the most anthropomorphic behaviour; for 9 of 14 behaviours >=50% of instances first appear after turn 1; anthropomorphic behaviour in one turn raises the likelihood in the next; high-frequency condition rated more anthropomorphic (Godspeed 4.00 vs 3.25; U = 213636, p < .001, r = .411) and more implicitly human-framed (AnthroScore, p < .05).
limitations_stated_by_authors: English and Western focus; one type of user simulation; only five turns; non-adversarial dialogues are not an upper bound; human agreement poor to moderate for subjective behaviours (empathy lowest)
relevance_to_cross_lingual_research: Authors state some behaviours (first-person pronouns, internal states) may generalize while norms for validation, empathy and emotional expression vary across cultures, and call for non-English validation. REVIEWER NOTE: the first-person measure is an English pronoun regex and would need a language-specific operationalization.
charting_status: Charted from arXiv 2502.07077v3 (camera-ready, 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026'). AI-assisted extraction, pending author verification.
